name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Wednesday 6 April 1983

clue.text: In the past, GPO's re sorted to temporary expedients

indicators.note: split from 'resorted', the words say the letters are sorted again into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
the General Post Office with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A nostalgic complaint that the old General Post Office used to make do with makeshift fixes.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'resorted' as 're sorted' and it stops being a verb of desperation and becomes the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Stopgaps are makeshift measures used until something permanent can be arranged.

clue.text: Silly toper holds forehead

indicators.note: a drinker who holds something has it inside him

blocks.note: a toper and a sot are both habitual drunks
read as fore-head: the head, or first letter, of fore

explanation.surface: A foolish drunk clutches his brow, presumably nursing a hangover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forehead' has to be split into 'fore' and 'head': the head of fore.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft can mean feeble-minded or foolish, as in 'soft in the head'.

clue.text: Harangue in "Love on the Dole"?

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O
a ration is an allowance doled out

explanation.surface: A rant delivered in Love on the Dole, Walter Greenwood's 1933 novel of Depression-era unemployment.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it a title, but break it up: 'on' simply places one piece before the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A harangue is a long, forceful speech, and an oration is a formal public address.

clue.text: Non-Spanish-speaking Americans in Gateshead, signor? That's odd!

indicators.note: something odd is out of its normal shape, so the Italian title is put into another order

blocks.note: the head of Gates, its first letter
the Italian form of address, taken as written

explanation.surface: An Italian gentleman is surprised to find English-speaking Americans in Gateshead, a town in north-east England.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead must be split into 'Gates' and 'head', the head of Gates.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin America gringo is a slang term for a foreigner, especially an English-speaking North American.

clue.text: Questionable letters from Price to Lamb

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of the words that follow, in any order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Doubtful correspondence between two people, perhaps the essayist Charles Lamb and a friend called Price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' looks like correspondence; it means the alphabetic letters of the names.
explanation.definitionFit: Something problematic is open to doubt or dispute, hard to settle.

clue.text: Infer member is a country type?

indicators.note: the opening word, split off from the rest of 'Infer', places the next item inside what follows

blocks.note: read as 'In fer': the word after 'In' is the outer part
an arm is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: Someone concludes that a particular club member must be a rustic sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Infer' must be broken in two: 'In' is the instruction, 'fer' the outer letters, with the member going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmer works the land, the archetypal rural person in contrast to a townsman.

clue.text: It's very hard for girl to master book, in short

definitions.note: a phrase for a noun: a very hard substance

blocks.note: a girl's name
Master of Arts
New Testament, abbreviated

explanation.surface: It is tough for a young woman to get to grips with a book, briefly put.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant is a legendary substance of supreme hardness, once identified with diamond.

clue.text: Unit Mao mobilised was revered by some Indians

definitions.note: a phrase for a noun: something revered

indicators.note: troops mobilised are moved about and redeployed, so these letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Chinese army unit raised by Chairman Mao was held in reverence on the subcontinent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indians' points to Asia after Mao, but these are Native Americans.
explanation.definitionFit: Manitou is the Algonquian name for a spirit or supernatural power venerated by several Native American peoples.

clue.text: Thinking Muir arranged to meet people?

indicators.note: arranged means set out in a chosen order, so the Scottish name is reordered

blocks.note: the Scottish surname, taken as written
a nation is a people

explanation.surface: Someone called Muir is planning to get together with others.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumination is deep, prolonged reflection, chewing a matter over in the mind.

clue.text: Note club for some evening out

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a noun

blocks.note: a flat is a note lowered by a semitone
an iron is a kind of golf club

explanation.surface: Someone notes down a club venue for a night on the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evening out' looks like a social night out; here it means making things even, as with creased cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatiron is an old-fashioned iron heated on a stove and used to smooth creases from laundry.

clue.text: Heathen MP — anyone differ?

indicators.note: if the letters differ from how they stand, they have been put in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
split as 'any' plus 'one', with one written as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A godless member of parliament challenges the house to disagree with him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyone' has to be split into 'any' and 'one', and one becomes the numeral I.
explanation.definitionFit: Paynim is an archaic word for a pagan or non-Christian, often used of Muslims in medieval romance.

clue.text: Author upset Antrim editor

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and jumbled, so the following place name is rearranged

blocks.note: Charles Kingsley, author of The Water-Babies and Westward Ho!
the Northern Irish county, taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer has annoyed a newspaper editor from County Antrim in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Author' looks like the definition but supplies the first name; the editor is Kingsley Martin.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley Martin edited the New Statesman, the British weekly political magazine, from 1930 to 1960.

clue.text: Cowardly sort of onset in the park

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant version, so the word's letters appear in a varied order

blocks.note: yellow is slang for cowardly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A timid kind of attack takes place in a public garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellowstone, in Wyoming, was the world's first national park.

clue.text: Speaking generally, Lady North is out of place in the vessel

indicators.note: letters out of place have left their positions, so they must be reordered
placing the scrambled letters in the craft puts them inside it

blocks.note: a barge is a flat-bottomed boat
LADY plus N, the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Broadly speaking, Lady North feels awkward aboard the boat.
explanation.definitionFit: By and large is an idiom meaning on the whole, in general terms.

clue.text: Pulls in the natives, some say

blocks.note: first meaning: tugs sharply
second meaning: the slang name some people use for Americans

explanation.surface: Someone tugs local people into a place, or so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some say' marks a nickname, not a sound-alike: Yanks is what some people call people born in the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: To yank is to jerk or tug hard, and Yanks is informal slang for Americans, especially in British usage.

clue.text: Hope the sporting body's entering the race

indicators.note: one thing entering another goes inside it, so the body goes into the race

blocks.note: the TT, or Tourist Trophy, is the Isle of Man motorcycle race
RU is Rugby Union, plus the possessive s

explanation.surface: A sports governing body puts its hopes in an entry for the big race.
explanation.definitionFit: To trust is to rely confidently on something happening, much as to hope for it.

clue.text: Film star in the house?

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a noun, fair because it describes something found in a house, which the question mark flags

blocks.note: first meaning: the Hollywood actor Clark ...
second meaning: a part of a building's roof

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a celebrity in the audience; the second half points at an architectural feature instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Clark Gable starred in Gone with the Wind, and a gable is the triangular wall end under a pitched roof.

clue.text: Money put on by backer?

blocks.note: surface reading: a sponsor putting up funds
setter's reading: paper money laid on a horse by a punter

explanation.walkthrough: A backer is both a financial sponsor and someone who backs a horse; either way the cash is paper money.
explanation.definitionFit: Banknotes are paper currency, the cash a punter hands over when placing a bet.

clue.text: Roll for visitor to Dingley Dell?

blocks.note: first meaning: to move along on wheels
second meaning: a guest at Mr Wardle's farm in Dickens's Pickwick Papers

explanation.walkthrough: Dingley Dell is the Wardles' country home in The Pickwick Papers; Mr Trundle courts and marries Isabella Wardle there.
explanation.definitionFit: To trundle is to roll slowly and heavily, and Trundle is a guest in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: Fish with the rest, possibly, given permit

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several possible versions of the word, so its letters can be reordered

blocks.note: the word rest; 'the' is part of the phrase
to let is to allow

explanation.surface: An angler is allowed to fish along with everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: The sterlet is a small sturgeon of the Caspian and Black Sea rivers, prized for caviar.

clue.text: Quiet producer of 17

blocks.note: first meaning: the musical direction to play softly
second meaning: a keyboard instrument that sounds musical tones, the other sense of 17's answer

explanation.walkthrough: 17's answer meant money there; here it is read as musical sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano is the Italian score marking for soft playing, and the piano is the instrument whose keys sound musical tones.

clue.text: Delighted to be among people, as Edward was?

indicators.note: the answer is to be found among the words that follow, sitting inside them

blocks.note: read straight through, ignoring the comma and spaces

explanation.surface: Edward enjoyed mixing with people, and someone wonders if anyone else felt the same.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'as Edward was' suggest a historical allusion, but the answer simply sits across the words, from the end of 'people' into 'Edward'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleased means glad or happy, a close synonym for delighted.

clue.text: Isn't commonly about the East, of course

definitions.note: a phrase for a noun: a racecourse

blocks.note: ain't is the colloquial form of isn't
re means concerning
E is the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A folksy denial about the East, with an 'of course' tacked on for emphasis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as a throwaway phrase; it means 'a course', here a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree, near Liverpool, is the racecourse that hosts the Grand National steeplechase.

clue.text: Censure eternal mistakes by author

indicators.note: used as a verb, to mistake the words is to get them wrong, which scrambles their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic condemns the never-ending errors in some writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mistakes' reads as a noun after 'eternal' but is the verb that does the jumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Sterne was the eighteenth-century Irish-born novelist who wrote Tristram Shandy.

clue.text: Employed an American journalist?

blocks.note: US is short for American
ed is short for editor

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a US reporter was taken on for the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the past tense of use, not the hiring of a reporter.
explanation.definitionFit: Used and employed both mean put to service or made use of.

clue.text: Gets free, having led revolution — that's puzzling

definitions.note: a phrase for a noun: something puzzling

indicators.note: a revolution turns the word round like a wheel, carrying its final letter up to the front

blocks.note: to rid is to free, as in getting rid of
the word revolved one place, its last letter moving to the front

explanation.surface: Someone frees themselves after heading an uprising, and the outcome baffles everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' tempts a solver to reverse the word; it rotates it instead, the last letter swinging round to lead.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a baffling question or enigma, anything that leaves you puzzled.

clue.text: New NCO classifies ships, perhaps

indicators.note: a new version of the letters means they have been remade in another order

blocks.note: a non-commissioned officer, taken as written
to sort is to classify into groups

explanation.surface: A newly promoted sergeant sorts the fleet into categories.
explanation.definitionFit: Consorts are ships sailing in company with each other, a sense found mostly in naval history.

clue.text: They happen to have seen TV variety

indicators.note: a variety of something is a different form, so the letters take a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Some people just happen to have caught a television variety show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety' looks like the variety show they watched; it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Events are occurrences, the things that take place or come about.

clue.text: Non-paying theatre-goer — Dr Arnold, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: someone admitted on a free ticket
second meaning, split in two: a headmaster who is no longer living

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arnold was the famous nineteenth-century headmaster of Rugby School, so read the answer as two words: a head now dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadhead is slang for someone using a free pass to a show, and the late Dr Arnold was a head teacher.
